opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what actually moves the needle for users. With audio it's very easy to get pulled in many directions at once: speech recognition, speech generation, full-duplex conversation, music, audio understanding more broadly. You can't do all of it at the same depth, especially as a relatively small team, so we try to ask: what capability, if we got it really right, would unlock the most downstream use cases?

For us that has mostly meant focusing on robust understanding first. If the model can't reliably transcribe and understand speech across accents, noisy environments, long recordings, and many languages, then everything you build on top of it is fragile. So a lot of priority goes into the unglamorous parts: data quality, evaluation across languages, and making sure we aren't overfitting to a couple of clean benchmarks that don't reflect real usage.

The second principle is that we try to keep audio close to the main language model effort rather than treating it as a separate silo. A lot of the gains come from the backbone getting better: better reasoning, better multilingual ability. So we want the audio work to inherit those improvements, and the audio team spends a lot of time on how to integrate the modality cleanly, not on reinventing everything from scratch.

Third, we like to keep a mix of short-term and longer-term bets. Some people are working on things we know we can ship in a few months, and some are exploring more speculative directions, like more natural real-time interaction, where it's not yet clear what the right architecture is. I think you need both. If everything is short-term you never get the step changes, and if everything is long-term you don't learn from real users.

Finally, evaluation drives a lot of it. Often the way we decide what to work on next is by looking hard at where the model fails, building good evals for those failure modes, and letting that tell us where the biggest gaps are. It sounds simple, but having trustworthy evals is probably the single most important thing for setting priorities well.

r001.rationale: The response names full-duplex conversation as one audio direction, then says the team has mostly focused on robust understanding first and treats natural real-time interaction as a longer-term bet. This communicates that they are not starting by building the full-duplex model.

fable-5.1.text:
So honestly, the first thing I'd say is that I don't think of it as "setting priorities" from the top. At Mistral we started very small, and the audio team is still small compared to what you'd find at the big labs, so you can't afford to be scattered. The constraint actually forces the discipline.

The way we think about it is roughly in two layers. The first is: what are the fundamental problems where we believe we can make real progress, not incremental progress? For audio that means things like speech recognition quality on languages that aren't English, latency for real-time interaction, and making the models small enough that people can actually run them, including on-device. Those are not sexy, but they're the things that matter if you want audio to be a real product rather than a demo.

The second layer is feedback from people using the models. We release open weights, and that gives us an enormous signal. People tell us very quickly where things break: accents, noisy environments, code-switching between French and Arabic, whatever it is. I'd rather have the roadmap driven by failure cases than by a slide deck.

And then there's a cultural piece, which I care about a lot. We hire people who are very strong technically and we give them a lot of freedom. If a researcher has a conviction about something, say a new architecture for streaming, I don't want to be the one who says no just because it's not on the plan. Some of the best things we've shipped came from someone being stubborn for a few weeks. My job is mostly to make sure that the few big bets we take are coherent with each other and with the rest of the models, so audio isn't a separate island from the text and multimodal work.

So: few bets, open release as a feedback loop, and trust the people. That's basically it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses audio research priorities and real-time interaction, but it does not state that the team will avoid starting by building a full-duplex audio model.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is to start with the capability we want to unlock. What would make the experience meaningfully better for someone using the model? With audio, that might be understanding speech in difficult conditions, generating more natural speech, or making the interaction fast enough that it feels like a conversation.

Then you work backward: what is actually preventing us from getting there? Is it the data, the model, or how we're evaluating it? I like research projects where we have a clear hypothesis and can run an experiment that tells us whether we're moving in the right direction.

And you need some room for ideas that are less predictable. If every project has an obvious outcome, you're probably being too conservative. So it's a balance between improving the things we know matter and exploring things that could change what we're able to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting from desired capabilities and working backward, but it does not state that the team will avoid beginning directly with a full-duplex audio model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what is the capability we want to unlock? With audio, that can mean several different things—understanding speech, generating speech, or having a conversation where the timing feels natural. Those lead to different research priorities.

Then I like to identify the main bottleneck and run a small experiment that can tell us whether an approach is promising. You want a clear feedback loop before committing a lot of compute. And you need to listen to the model, because a benchmark score doesn’t capture everything about an audio interaction. A system can get the words right and still feel awkward to talk to.

So it’s a balance between pursuing longer-term ideas and fixing the limitations that prevent the system from being useful today.

r001.rationale: The response recommends identifying a capability and testing bottlenecks before committing compute, but it does not state that the team will avoid starting directly with a full-duplex audio model.
